summary: Phil Hetzel leads solutions engineering at BrainTrust, an agent quality platform focused on two pillars: evals for pre-production experimentation confidence and observability for post-production confidence. With 12 years in consulting, including leading the global Databricks business unit at Slalom Consulting, he observed customers excelling at GenAI proofs of concept but struggling with production deployment. He identifies two organizational types: traditional enterprises, where leadership delegates GenAI to existing ML or data science teams because generative AI has AI in the name, and AI natives, smaller cross-functional teams with closer proximity to end-user problems who built their offerings around agents from the start. Hetzel highlights key differences between traditional ML and GenAI: the model is already built by companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Mistral, eliminating the training data pipeline. Behavior changes come through prompt and context engineering rather than feature engineering or retraining. He presents the case for data scientists owning agents—understanding neural networks, possessing rigorous governance processes, and having testing mindsets—and the counterpoint that with models pre-built, traditional cross-validation is unnecessary and data scientists may fixate on precision, recall, and F1 rather than functional agent performance. He then argues for a diverse team: product engineers are adept at API integration, complex agents involve distributed systems challenges, and subject matter experts should control prompts and contribute to human annotation. In the final section, Hetzel identifies specific ways data scientists add value: providing guardrails by understanding LLMs are statistical token predictors, applying expertise to LLM-as-judge eval processes with labeled datasets, and fine-tuning open-source models. The ideal mix includes product, application, and systems engineers implementing requirements; non-technical experts performing human annotation and prompt/context engineering; and eval and observability pipelines providing production feedback loops. During Q&A, an audience member reframes agents as tools to solve problems rather than something to be owned by one team, which Hetzel endorses, noting the mistake is isolating agent development to ML engineers as if building another predictive model. Another question about BrainTrust's tooling reveals the platform includes human labeling, an agent and prompt playground for domain experts, and production data collection to continually enrich offline eval datasets and check whether evals align with human agreement.

sections.title: Introduction and BrainTrust Overview
sections.summary: Phil Hetzel introduces himself as solutions engineering lead at BrainTrust, an agent quality platform with two pillars: evals for pre-production experimentation confidence and observability for post-production confidence. He shares his background in consulting, including leading the global Databricks business unit at Slalom, and notes customers struggled moving GenAI proofs of concept to production.

sections.title: Organizational Approaches to Agentic Development
sections.summary: Hetzel contrasts traditional enterprises, where leadership delegates GenAI to existing ML or data science teams because it has AI in the name, with AI-native companies that use small cross-functional teams with closer proximity to the problems agents are meant to solve.

sections.title: Traditional ML vs Generative AI Differences
sections.summary: He explains that traditional ML involves a data pipeline of training, testing, and deployment, while in GenAI the model is already built by providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Mistral. Behavior changes come through prompt and context engineering rather than feature engineering or retraining, though teams still need to perform evals after implementing APIs.

sections.title: Case For and Against Data Scientists Owning Agents
sections.summary: Hetzel presents arguments for data scientists: they understand neural networks, have rigorous governance processes, and possess testing mindsets. Counterarguments: models are pre-built, traditional cross-validation is unnecessary, and data scientists may fixate on precision, recall, and F1 rather than functional agent performance. He argues for including non-data scientists: product engineers handle APIs well, complex agents involve distributed systems challenges, and subject matter experts should control prompts and contribute to human annotation.

sections.title: How Data Scientists Add Value and Ideal Team Mix
sections.summary: Hetzel identifies three ways data scientists add value: providing guardrails by grounding LLM understanding as statistical token prediction, applying expertise to LLM-as-judge eval processes with labeled datasets and precision/recall/F1 measurement, and fine-tuning open-source models for specific use cases. The ideal team mix includes product, application, and systems engineers implementing requirements; non-technical experts performing human annotation and prompt/context engineering; and eval and observability pipelines for production feedback loops.

sections.title: Q&A: Agents as Tools and BrainTrust Tooling
sections.summary: During Q&A, an audience member reframes agents as tools to solve problems rather than something owned by one team, which Hetzel endorses, noting the mistake is isolating development to ML engineers as if building another predictive model. Another question about BrainTrust's tooling reveals the platform includes human labeling, an agent and prompt playground for domain experts to experiment, and production data collection to continually enrich offline eval datasets and check whether evals align with or diverge from human agreement.

limitations: Traditional enterprises struggle to move GenAI from proof of concept to production

evidence.supports: Traditional enterprises delegate GenAI to ML/data science teams based on naming rather than skill alignment

evidence.excerpt: Anthropic and OpenAI and Mistral, they've already done the the data process of um grabbing that data, putting it through the pipeline, training the underlying LLM
evidence.supports: The traditional ML data pipeline is already completed by model providers

evidence.excerpt: the way that you can change that behavior is just by changing the inputs, the prompts, the context that you're giving that that model
evidence.supports: GenAI behavior is modified through prompt and context engineering rather than retraining

evidence.excerpt: they will really lock on to the traditional ML engineer metrics like precision, recall, F1, um and they'll obsess over those metrics
evidence.supports: Data scientists may inappropriately apply traditional ML metrics to agent evaluation

evidence.excerpt: LLMs are just APIs. Product engineers are very used to using APIs as they as they build applications
evidence.supports: Product engineers are well-suited for GenAI development because LLMs are API-based

evidence.excerpt: it is far broader of a surface area that you need to be evaluating. You need to be evaluating the functional uh performance of that agent
evidence.supports: Agent evaluation requires functional performance assessment across a broader surface area than traditional ML metrics

evidence.excerpt: data scientists can add um to to use an overloaded term, add the guardrails to this process. A lot of people are very aggressive in in how they implement LLMs. They don't understand how the underlying technology works.
evidence.supports: Data scientists provide guardrails by bringing statistical understanding of how LLMs work

evidence.excerpt: LLM as judge is a huge part of the eval process when you're building agentic applications. Um, again, people are very tempted to just believe LLM as judges when they're performing evals. They're just prompts and models at the end of the day
evidence.supports: LLM-as-judge is important in eval but data scientists can apply rigorous metrics to validate it

evidence.excerpt: if you do need to fine-tune an open-source model very specifically to your use case, that's probably going to be like the most fun and and technical thing where uh data scientists and machine learning engineers can can add a ton of value
evidence.supports: Fine-tuning open-source models is a key area where data scientists and ML engineers add technical value

evidence.excerpt: I think the mistake that I see a lot of typically traditional companies make is they say, 'Oh, this is we're making another predictive model.' And they isolate it to the ML engineers or data scientists and say, 'Go build and go build these agent things.'

evidence.excerpt: We do have a human labeling component as a part of our platform and we do have like a agent and prompt playground where people can experiment with their own prompts and send them to the underlying agents themselves.
evidence.supports: BrainTrust provides human labeling and prompt playground features for domain expert involvement

evidence.excerpt: we gather data from production to continually add to that offline data set that we're evaluating upon. And then, hopefully, we're gaining grounded data along the way where we can kind of self-check ourselves to understand um if our evals are aligning
